# Arranging Numbers 2 to 2022 with Divisibility Constraints

## Setting Up the Problem

I need to place the numbers $\{2, 3, 4, \ldots, 2022\}$ (2021 numbers) into positions $1, 2, \ldots, 2021$ such that position $i$ contains a multiple of $i$.

## Key Structural Insight

I'll model this as a directed graph: draw an edge from position $i$ to number $f(i)$. Since $f$ is a bijection from $\{1,\ldots,2021\}$ to $\{2,\ldots,2022\}$, this forms a collection of cycles and paths.

**No cycles are possible:** A cycle $i_1 \to i_2 \to \cdots \to i_k \to i_1$ (with all $i_j \geq 2$) would require $i_j \mid i_{j+1}$ for all $j$, forcing $i_1 = i_2 = \cdots = i_k$ (a contradiction for a proper cycle).

**Therefore, the only non-trivial structure is a single path from position 1 to number 2022:**

$$1 \to n_1 \to n_2 \to \cdots \to n_m \to 2022$$

where $2 \leq n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_m \leq 2021$, with $n_j \mid n_{j+1}$ and $n_m \mid 2022$. All other positions get their own number.

## Counting Valid Chains

Since $n_m \mid 2022$ and $n_m \leq 2021$, I need $n_m$ to be a **proper divisor of 2022 that is $\geq 2$**.

$$2022 = 2 \times 3 \times 337 \quad \text{(all prime)}$$

The proper divisors $\geq 2$ are: $\{2, 3, 6, 337, 674, 1011\}$.

For each endpoint $d$, I count chains $2 \leq a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k = d$ where $a_j \mid a_{j+1}$:

| Endpoint $d$ | Valid chains | Count |
|:---:|:---|:---:|
| $2$ | $[2]$ | 1 |
| $3$ | $[3]$ | 1 |
| $6$ | $[6],\; [2,6],\; [3,6]$ | 3 |
| $337$ | $[337]$ | 1 |
| $674 = 2 \times 337$ | $[674],\; [2,674],\; [337,674]$ | 3 |
| $1011 = 3 \times 337$ | $[1011],\; [3,1011],\; [337,1011]$ | 3 |

**Total non-trivial arrangements:** $1 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 3 = 12$

## Verification of a Non-Trivial Arrangement

Take the chain $1 \to 337 \to 674 \to 2022$:
- Position 1 gets 337: $1 \mid 337$ ✓  
- Position 337 gets 674: $337 \mid 674$ (since $674 = 2 \times 337$) ✓  
- Position 674 gets 2022: $674 \mid 2022$ (since $2022 = 3 \times 674$) ✓  
- All other positions $i$ get $i$ ✓  
- Every number in $\{2,\ldots,2022\}$ used exactly once ✓

## Final Count

$$\underbrace{1}_{\text{trivial: } 1\to 2022} + \underbrace{12}_{\text{non-trivial chains}} = 13$$

$$\boxed{13}$$
